extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners and journalism researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Designing press releases so their key claims and framing survive journalists' transformation into news copy, maximizing pickup and fidelity. Based on discourse-analysis evidence of which textual slots (headline, lead, quotes, statistics, context) are most likely to be reproduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survival-of-quoted-material
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct quotes from the release are the most likely segment to survive into news verbatim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pickup-worthy release uses its quote slot to deliver the message-payload; craft quotes to encapsulate the core claim or soundbite you want reproduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline-as-template
rubrics_metrics.description: Release headlines that are publishable as wire headlines are reproduced more often.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the release headline as a complete subject–verb–object structure ready to print (i.e., a wire-ready headline) so journalists can reuse it with minimal editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead-survival
rubrics_metrics.description: The first 35 words of the release survive into news at the highest rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put maximum information density into the lead (first ~35 words) so the most important facts are likely to be carried into coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-canned context paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Background/context paragraphs (e.g., 'Company X is the largest...', 'Y disease affects 1.3 million Americans...') are replicated when supplied; without them journalists either omit context (degrading coverage) or invent context (introducing error).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide ready-made context paragraphs to ensure accurate background is reproduced rather than omitted or inaccurately invented by journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote attribution clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes survive most reliably when attributed to a single named, titled source rather than to 'a spokesperson.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute quotes to a specific person with title to increase the chance the quote (and its source) is copied verbatim into news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedded statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical claims survive intact; rhetorical claims get rewritten or dropped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include precise numerical/statistical claims where possible, since numbers are more likely to be carried over verbatim than vague rhetorical language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of insider register
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases written in industry jargon trigger journalist rewriting (with attendant slippage); plain-register releases survive intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain, non‑technical language rather than insider jargon to reduce the need for journalist rewriting and preserve intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single message frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists adopt the release's frame when the release commits to one; releases that hedge across multiple frames cede the framing decision back to the journalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commit to a single, clear framing for your message if you want journalists to reproduce that frame; avoid hedging across incompatible frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag_sponsoring_interest_and_supply_context (ethical caveat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Churnalism erodes journalistic agenda-setting; a pickup-worthy and democratically-responsible release flags its sponsoring interest and supplies enough context for the journalist to interrogate, even when copy-paste use is enabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about who is behind the release and include sufficient contextual information so journalists (and readers) can assess interests and claims—this balances pickup with ethical responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place_high-value_claims_in_load-bearing_slots
rubrics_metrics.description: Textual elements designed by the PR writer (headline, lead, quote, statistics, context paragraph) are the elements most likely to survive the transformation pipeline into news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategically place your most important claims and factual payloads in those 'load-bearing' slots (headline, opening ~35 words, quoted material, embedded statistics, and pre-canned context) to maximize both pickup and fidelity of representation.
